familyProfiles/east-syriac/tagline: The Syriac church of Persia that once reached China and India.
familyProfiles/east-syriac/summary: The church of the Persian Empire and beyond, using East Syriac liturgy and the theology of Theodore of Mopsuestia. In the Middle Ages it was the most widespread church in Asia; today it survives in the Assyrian Church of the East, the Ancient Church of the East and, in communion with Rome, the Chaldean and Syro-Malabar churches.
familyProfiles/east-syriac/story:
Christianity reached Mesopotamia and Persia very early, through Edessa and the Jewish communities of the region. Under Sasanian rule the church organised itself at the Synod of Seleucia-Ctesiphon in 410, under a catholicos who later took the title of patriarch, and in 424 declared itself independent of the 'Western' fathers. At Beth Lapat (484) it adopted the theology of Theodore of Mopsuestia, which stressed the full humanity of Christ; outsiders, wrongly in the church's view, called it 'Nestorian'.

From its school at Nisibis and its monasteries the church sent missionaries along the Silk Road. The monk Alopen reached the Tang capital Chang'an in 635, as recorded on the Xi'an stele of 781; there were bishops in Central Asia, among the Turks and Mongols, in Tibet, and among the Thomas Christians of India, who received their bishops from Mesopotamia until the sixteenth century. At its height in the thirteenth century the patriarch oversaw perhaps more than two hundred dioceses.

Decline came with the conversion of the Mongol khans to Islam, the plague and the campaigns of Timur (c. 1400), which left the church confined to the mountains of Kurdistan and northern Iraq. A dispute over hereditary succession in 1552 led part of the church into union with Rome as the Chaldean Catholic Church, while in India the Portuguese latinised the Thomas Christians at the Synod of Diamper (1599).

In the twentieth century the Assyrian community suffered massacres during and after the First World War, and the patriarchate moved into exile, residing in Chicago from 1940 before returning to Erbil in 2015. A dispute over the Gregorian calendar and hereditary succession produced the Ancient Church of the East in 1968. War in Iraq and Syria since 2003 has scattered much of the remaining population; the faithful now live largely in diaspora in North America, Europe and Australia.

The church's legacy is immense for its size: the first Christian mission to China, the Syriac literature of Narsai and Isaac of Nineveh, and the ancestry of India's Thomas Christians. The Common Christological Declaration signed by Pope John Paul II and Patriarch Mar Dinkha IV in 1994 acknowledged that both churches confess the same faith in Christ.
familyProfiles/east-syriac/origin/event: Synod of Isaac organises the church of the Persian Empire under its own catholicos.
familyProfiles/east-syriac/coreDoctrines: Christ is one person (parsopa) in two natures (kyane), each with its own properties.
Mary is 'Mother of Christ' rather than 'Mother of God', a title the church avoids though it does not deny the deity of the one she bore.
Sacraments ('mysteries'), including the Holy Leaven (Malka) handed down in tradition.
Authority of Scripture as read by Theodore of Mopsuestia and the Syriac Fathers.
familyProfiles/east-syriac/focuses/0: East Syriac liturgy of Addai and Mari, one of the oldest Eucharistic prayers in use.
familyProfiles/east-syriac/focuses/1: Preservation of Assyrian language and identity.
familyProfiles/east-syriac/focuses/2: Monasticism and the mystical theology of Isaac of Nineveh.
familyProfiles/east-syriac/focuses/3: Care for refugee and diaspora communities.
familyProfiles/east-syriac/strengths/0: Historic missionary reach across Asia unmatched before modern times.
familyProfiles/east-syriac/strengths/2: Resilience after repeated persecution and exile.
familyProfiles/east-syriac/strengths/3: Productive dialogue with the Catholic Church since 1994.
familyProfiles/east-syriac/criticisms/0: Byzantine and Latin churches long condemned it as Nestorian.
familyProfiles/east-syriac/criticisms/2: Small and fragmented today, with communities scattered by war.
familyProfiles/east-syriac/internalDivis: Opponents of hereditary succession elected Yohannan Sulaqa, who entered communion with Rome (later the Chaldean Catholic Church).
Portuguese authorities brought Kerala's Thomas Christians under Latin control, cutting ties with the East Syriac patriarch.
Split over the adoption of the Gregorian calendar and hereditary succession; reunion talks continue.
A small Assyrian-linked community in Thrissur, the main surviving East Syriac body in India.
familyProfiles/east-syriac/influencedFam: The Chaldean and Syro-Malabar Catholic churches keep the East Syriac rite.
Kerala's Thomas Christians who rejected Latin rule (1653) later adopted West Syriac Orthodox ties.
Its Syriac Fathers preserve an early, Semitic form of Christian thought.
familyProfiles/lutheran/tagline: Justification by faith alone, preached and sung since Wittenberg.
familyProfiles/lutheran/summary: The churches that follow the teaching of Martin Luther and the Augsburg Confession (1530), centred on justification by grace through faith and the real presence of Christ in the Lord's Supper. They range from national folk churches in Scandinavia to fast-growing churches in Ethiopia, Tanzania and Indonesia.
familyProfiles/lutheran/story:
Lutheranism began with Martin Luther's protest against indulgences in his Ninety-Five Theses (1517) at Wittenberg. Excommunicated in 1521, Luther translated the Bible into German, reformed the Mass and wrote catechisms (1529) that shaped generations. The Augsburg Confession, presented by Philip Melanchthon to Charles V in 1530, became the defining statement of faith, and the Book of Concord (1580) gathered the Lutheran confessions.

The Reformation spread through the German princes and cities, legally recognised at the Peace of Augsburg (1555), and became the established religion of Denmark–Norway, Sweden–Finland and the Baltic lands. Emigration carried Lutherans to North America, Australia and southern Brazil, while missions from Halle and later from Leipzig, Hermannsburg and Scandinavia took the faith to India (Tranquebar, 1706), southern Africa, Tanzania, Ethiopia, Namibia, Madagascar, Papua New Guinea and Sumatra.

After Luther's death his followers divided between strict 'Gnesio-Lutherans' and Melanchthon's 'Philippists' until the Formula of Concord (1577). Pietism, launched by Philipp Jakob Spener's Pia Desideria (1675), stressed personal conversion against a cold orthodoxy. The Prussian Union of Lutheran and Reformed churches (1817) drove confessional 'Old Lutherans' to emigrate, helping found the conservative Lutheran Church–Missouri Synod (1847). In the twentieth century Lutherans divided over biblical criticism, women's ordination and sexuality.

The Lutheran World Federation's 150 member churches reported about 78.4 million members in 2023. Africa now has the most (about 30.8 million), led by the Ethiopian Evangelical Church Mekane Yesus; the Nordic countries (about 17.2 million) and Germany still have large if declining folk churches, and there are significant churches in Tanzania, Indonesia (the Batak HKBP) and India.

Lutheranism gave Protestantism its first theology, the vernacular hymn and chorale (culminating in J. S. Bach), the model of the territorial church, and thinkers such as Kierkegaard and Bonhoeffer. The Joint Declaration on the Doctrine of Justification (1999) with the Catholic Church marked a milestone in healing the division that Luther began.
familyProfiles/lutheran/origin/event: Martin Luther publishes his Ninety-Five Theses against indulgences.
familyProfiles/lutheran/coreDoctrines/0: Justification by grace alone through faith alone, on account of Christ alone.
familyProfiles/lutheran/coreDoctrines/1: Scripture as the sole norm of faith, read through the Lutheran confessions (Book of Concord, 1580).
familyProfiles/lutheran/coreDoctrines/2: Law and Gospel distinguished as God's two words.
familyProfiles/lutheran/coreDoctrines/3: Baptism (including of infants) and the Lord's Supper as means of grace.
familyProfiles/lutheran/coreDoctrines/4: Real presence: Christ's body and blood are truly present 'in, with and under' the bread and wine.
familyProfiles/lutheran/coreDoctrines/5: The priesthood of all baptised believers and the doctrine of vocation.
familyProfiles/lutheran/focuses/0: Preaching of the Gospel and liturgical worship.
familyProfiles/lutheran/focuses/3: Diakonia: social service and relief (e.g. LWF World Service).
familyProfiles/lutheran/focuses/4: Ecumenical dialogue, notably with Catholics and Anglicans.
familyProfiles/lutheran/strengths/2: Balance of liturgical tradition and evangelical preaching.
familyProfiles/lutheran/strengths/3: Rapid growth in Africa and Asia.
familyProfiles/lutheran/criticisms/0: Luther's late writings against Jews were later exploited by antisemites; the LWF repudiated them in 1984.
familyProfiles/lutheran/criticisms/1: State-church dependence fostered nominal membership in Europe.
familyProfiles/lutheran/criticisms/2: Many German Protestants accommodated to Nazism (with the Confessing Church as the exception).
familyProfiles/lutheran/criticisms/3: Sharp divisions between liberal and confessional bodies.
familyProfiles/lutheran/internalDivision: Quarrels after the Augsburg and Leipzig Interims, resolved by the Formula of Concord (1577).
Spener and Francke called for heartfelt faith and small groups, against Lutheran Orthodoxy.
Prussian Union and the Old Lutherans
Forced union with the Reformed led confessional Lutherans to resist and emigrate.
A Nordic revival movement that later split into several separate groups.
Missouri Synod faculty walk-out over biblical criticism; moderates later joined what became the ELCA.
The ELCA's decision to allow partnered gay clergy led to the formation of the North American Lutheran Church (2010).
familyProfiles/lutheran/influencedFamili: Cranmer and early English reformers borrowed Lutheran liturgy and doctrine.
Wesley's heart was 'strangely warmed' hearing Luther's preface to Romans read (1738).
Reformed Protestantism began in dialogue and debate with Luther.
Pietism and the Moravians transmitted a Lutheran stress on conversion to the evangelical revival.
familyProfiles/reformed/tagline: Calvinist churches of covenant, confession and the sovereignty of God.
familyProfiles/reformed/summary: The Protestant tradition that grew from Zwingli in Zurich and Calvin in Geneva, including Presbyterian, Reformed and Congregational churches. It emphasises God's sovereign grace, the authority of Scripture, a simple worship ordered by the Word, and government by elders.
familyProfiles/reformed/story:
The Reformed tradition began when Huldrych Zwingli started preaching through the Gospel of Matthew at Zurich's Grossmünster in 1519, and quickly took a more radical line than Luther on images, worship and the Lord's Supper. Its decisive centre became Geneva, where John Calvin's Institutes of the Christian Religion (1536, final edition 1559) and his church order (1541) offered a model of a reformed city and a training ground for pastors.

From Geneva the movement spread to France (the Huguenots), the Netherlands, the Palatinate, Hungary and Transylvania, and Scotland, where John Knox led the Reformation of 1560. It produced a wealth of confessions: the Belgic (1561), the Heidelberg Catechism (1563), the Second Helvetic (1566), the Canons of Dort (1619) and the Westminster Confession (1646). English Puritans and Congregationalists carried it to New England, and Dutch settlers to southern Africa and Indonesia.

The tradition's emphasis on confession and church discipline made it prone to division. The Synod of Dort rejected the Arminian Remonstrants (1618–19); English Puritans divided between Presbyterians and Independents; Scotland saw repeated secessions culminating in the Disruption of 1843. Modern quarrels over biblical criticism, the Fundamentalist–Modernist controversy, apartheid in South Africa and sexuality have produced further splits, alongside unions such as the Church of South India and the Protestant Church in the Netherlands.

The World Communion of Reformed Churches describes its member churches as representing about 100 million Christians. Today the strongest Reformed churches are often outside Europe: in South Korea, Indonesia, Nigeria, Ghana, Kenya, Brazil and the north-eastern Indian states of Mizoram and Meghalaya, as well as in the United States, Scotland, Switzerland, the Netherlands and Hungary.

Reformed thought shaped modern political ideas of covenant, limited government and the right of resistance, the Puritan work ethic made famous by Max Weber, and theologians from Jonathan Edwards to Abraham Kuyper and Karl Barth. Its influence runs through Baptist, evangelical and much of Anglican theology.
familyProfiles/reformed/origin/event: Huldrych Zwingli begins expository preaching at the Grossmünster, launching the Swiss Reformation.
familyProfiles/reformed/coreDoctrines/0: Scripture alone as the supreme rule of faith and worship (the 'regulative principle' in strict forms).
familyProfiles/reformed/coreDoctrines/1: The sovereignty of God in salvation: unconditional election and effectual grace (Canons of Dort).
familyProfiles/reformed/coreDoctrines/2: Covenant theology uniting the Old and New Testaments.
familyProfiles/reformed/coreDoctrines/3: Baptism of believers' children as a sign of the covenant.
familyProfiles/reformed/coreDoctrines/4: Christ is spiritually present in the Lord's Supper, received by faith through the Holy Spirit.
familyProfiles/reformed/coreDoctrines/5: Church government by elders (presbyters) in sessions, presbyteries and synods.
familyProfiles/reformed/focuses/2: Education: schools, universities and an educated ministry.
familyProfiles/reformed/focuses/3: Transforming society and culture under God's law.
familyProfiles/reformed/strengths/1: Strong tradition of education and literacy.
familyProfiles/reformed/strengths/2: Representative church government that influenced democratic institutions.
familyProfiles/reformed/strengths/3: Vigorous churches in Korea, Africa and Indonesia.
familyProfiles/reformed/criticisms/0: Doctrine of double predestination is rejected by Arminian, Catholic and Orthodox Christians.
familyProfiles/reformed/criticisms/1: Theocratic tendencies and harsh discipline in early Geneva, Scotland and New England.
familyProfiles/reformed/criticisms/2: Dutch Reformed theology was used to justify apartheid until the 1980s.
familyProfiles/reformed/internalDivision: The Synod of Dort condemned the Arminians, who formed the Remonstrant Brotherhood.
Westminster Assembly debates divided Presbyterians from Independents over church government.
About a third of Church of Scotland ministers left to form the Free Church over patronage and state control.
Dutch secessions (1834, 1886 under Kuyper) from the national Reformed church.
J. Gresham Machen and conservatives left the northern Presbyterian church over modernism.
Conservatives left the southern Presbyterian church; Korean Presbyterians also divided into many bodies.
Black Dutch Reformed churches in South Africa condemned apartheid theology.
familyProfiles/reformed/influencedFamili: Particular Baptists adopted Calvinist doctrine (Second London Confession, 1689).
Puritan and Reformed theology shaped the Great Awakening through Edwards and Whitefield.
The Thirty-Nine Articles reflect Reformed views of the Eucharist and predestination.
Reformed churches were central to most twentieth-century united churches.
The Campbells and Stone came from Presbyterian backgrounds.
